description: Our team is full and we are not accepting new members. We are a closed team of [medical students and developers] building a prototype onboard monitoring system for astronauts on deep-space missions. It tracks each astronaut against their own baseline for the headward fluid shift behind spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) and neck-vein stasis. It keeps a running risk estimate, decides when the next measurement is worth taking, and shows its reasoning when Earth cant reply
summary:
ASTROSENTINEL is a prototype onboard monitor for the headward fluid shift in astronauts: spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) and neck-vein stasis.
On Mars missions and beyond, communication delays of up to about 20 minutes each way mean the crew cannot wait for a flight surgeon. 
ASTROSENTINEL tracks each astronaut against their own baseline using optic nerve sheath diameter and jugular ultrasound measurements, keeps separate running risk estimates for SANS and venous stasis, and assigns a decision tier (Monitor, Repeat, Consult or Urgent) with its reasoning shown. 
"It never prescribes treatment".
 A crew view, a ground view with a 0 to 20 minute communication delay, and a 30-day mission playback demonstrate the loop. Because we have no real astronaut data, we built a simulated crew of 300 astronauts over 30 days, with hidden events as an answer key. 

All data is synthetic and the tool is not validated for clinical use. Early simulated tests show that when scans happen limits how fast events are detected, which motivates our adaptive scan trigger.
details:
A prototype onboard monitoring system that tracks headward fluid shift in astronauts, specifically targeting Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and neck-vein stasis. It uses a two-stage monitoring loop where daily weak signals, such as Heart Rate Variability (HRV) drift and pulse transit time, are compared against the astronaut's personal baseline. This triggers a decision on whether a confirmatory measurement, like optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) or internal jugular vein area, is needed sooner than a fixed schedule. The engine updates separate SANS and venous stasis risk probabilities and maps them to one of four decision tiers (Monitor, Repeat, Consult, Urgent).

The software dictates exactly when a measurement is worth taking, saving crew time and resources compared to a static scanning schedule. It escalates medical issues by displaying the underlying reasoning and evidence, allowing astronauts to make informed decisions when Earth cannot answer in time.

It operationalizes the per-astronaut longitudinal trending specified in NASA's Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) architecture, bridging the gap between raw hardware readings and autonomous clinical decision-making for fluid-shift pathology.


The backend simulation engine and trigger logic are built in Python, utilizing Pandas and SciPy for sequential risk updating and statistical drift detection. The frontend is an interactive web application developed using Streamlit, deployed via Vercel, and version-controlled through GitHub.


Instead of treating SANS and venous stasis as isolated problems or relying on point-in-time image analysis models, the software fuses both findings into a continuous, running risk estimate per astronaut. It approaches clinical decision-making creatively by using sequential risk updating—multiplying prior odds by the likelihood ratio of a new scan—to prevent a single anomalous reading from triggering a false alarm. Furthermore, it tests the novel hypothesis of linking daily wearable data directly to fluid-shift pathology within a simulated environment.
